report:
## Conclusion

The evidence is mixed and has shifted over time, so a firm "yes" is no longer warranted. Older, smaller meta-analyses (largely in children) suggested probiotics modestly shortened diarrhea duration by roughly 1 day. However, the updated **2020 Cochrane systematic review** (Collinson et al., 82 RCTs, ~12,000 participants) found that when large, high-quality, more recent trials were included, the overall benefit largely disappeared or became highly uncertain — probiotics probably make little or no difference to diarrhea duration, and the certainty of evidence is very low to moderate depending on the outcome (Cochrane, https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea).

This overturning of earlier positive conclusions was driven partly by two large, rigorous, placebo-controlled U.S. pediatric emergency department trials (Freedman et al. and Schnadower et al., NEJM 2018) that found *Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG* and a combination probiotic had **no significant effect** on diarrhea duration or severity in children with acute gastroenteritis (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598).

More recent, smaller meta-analyses continue to report modest benefits, particularly with specific strains or combinations in children (e.g., a 2024/2025 pediatric meta-analysis found "very low certainty" evidence of about one fewer day of diarrhea) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37956795/), and an emergency-medicine review concluded routine use is not recommended (https://www.annemergmed.com/article/S0196-0644(21)00116-5/fulltext).

**Bottom line:** Probiotics may modestly shorten diarrhea duration in some children by strain-specific effects, but the best current evidence (Cochrane 2020, large NEJM RCTs) shows this benefit is inconsistent, small, and of low certainty—routine use cannot be strongly recommended, especially in adults.
